passages.happening:
Abram leaves Egypt and goes back up into the Negev, the dry south, with Sarai, Lot and everything he owns (verse 1). He is now “extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold” (verse 2).

He travels north in stages until he reaches the place between Bethel and Ai where his tent had stood before, “to the site where he had built the altar” (verses 3-4). “And there Abram called on the name of the LORD” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers would notice where Abram goes. He does not just go back to Canaan. He goes back to the exact spot where he had built an altar before things went wrong in Egypt (12:8).

To ‘call on the name of the LORD’ means to pray and worship, speaking to God by his name. The same words describe the first worship of the LORD in 4:26. Abram's story in Egypt was full of his own plans. Here he starts again with worship.

The wealth is real, but the reader knows where some of it came from. Abram gained much of it in Egypt, because of the way he treated Sarai (12:16). Genesis lists the riches without praising them. The next verses will show what riches can do to a family.
passages.later:
The Bible often pictures turning back to God as going back to where you started. Jesus tells of a son who wasted everything and then “got up and went to his father” (Luke 15:20).

The church in Ephesus is told to “keep in mind how far you have fallen. Repent and perform the deeds you did at first” (Revelation 2:5). To repent means to turn around.

The prophet Jeremiah gives the same picture: “Stand at the crossroads and look. Ask for the ancient paths: ‘Where is the good way?’ Then walk in it” (Jeremiah 6:16).
passages.asks: After his failure in Egypt, Abram went back to the altar. Ask where you have drifted since you last truly prayed. Then ask what your ‘altar between Bethel and Ai’ would be: the place, the habit or the honest prayer where you could begin again.

passages.happening:
Lot also has flocks, herds and tents (verse 5). The land cannot feed them all, and their herdsmen start to quarrel (verses 6-7).

Abram says to Lot, “Please let there be no contention between you and me, or between your herdsmen and my herdsmen. After all, we are brothers” (verse 8). He offers Lot the first choice: “If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left” (verse 9).

Lot looks out and sees “the whole plain of the Jordan, all the way to Zoar, was well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt” (verse 10). He chooses it and moves east (verse 11). He pitches “his tent toward Sodom” (verse 12). Then a short sentence: “But the men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Herders needed grass and water, and both were scarce in the hill country. Quarrels over wells and grazing were common (see 21:25 and 26:20). When two households grew too big, they split up.

What is surprising is how Abram does it. He is the older man and the head of the family. By custom he had the right to choose first. Instead he lets Lot choose. ‘Brothers’ here means close relatives. Abram puts family peace ahead of property.

The Jordan plain looked like paradise. A reader in Canaan, where the crops depended on rain, would feel the pull of Lot's view. Eden was watered by rivers, and Egypt by the Nile. Both meant plenty that did not depend on the sky.

But the narrator adds a warning in brackets: this was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah. Where exactly those cities stood is not known. Scholars have proposed sites near both the south end and the north end of the Dead Sea, and there is no agreement.

Lot does not move into Sodom at once. He pitches his tent toward it. By chapter 14 he is living in it (14:12). The slide happens one step at a time.
passages.later:
Peter calls Lot “a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless” (2 Peter 2:7). He chose to live where his own soul was troubled day after day (2 Peter 2:8).

The prophet Ezekiel names the sin of Sodom: “She and her daughters were arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). The rich plain made people proud and hard toward the poor.

Paul's words fit Abram's offer: “in humility consider others more important than yourselves” (Philippians 2:3). And he says, “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18). Abram did not wait for Lot to make peace. He made it.
passages.asks: Lot chose by what he could see: good grass and plenty of water. He did not ask what kind of place Sodom was. Ask how you make your big choices: a job, a home, a friendship. Do you look only at what is good for your bank account, or also at what it will do to your soul?

passages.happening:
After Lot leaves, the LORD speaks to Abram. “Now lift up your eyes from the place where you are, and look to the north and south and east and west, for all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever” (verses 14-15).

God promises, “I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth” (verse 16). Then he says, “Get up and walk around the land, through its length and breadth, for I will give it to you” (verse 17).

Abram moves his tent to the Oaks of Mamre at Hebron, and builds an altar to the LORD there (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The story is told so that the reader compares two men looking. Lot ‘looked out’ and chose the best land for himself. Now God tells Abram to look, in every direction. Lot took what he saw. Abram is given what he sees.

Abram gave up his right to choose first. He did not lose anything by it. God gives him more than Lot took.

Walking through land could be a way of showing a claim to it. God later tells Joshua, “I have given you every place where the sole of your foot will tread” (Joshua 1:3).

Hebron is an old town in the hills south of Jerusalem. Mamre is close by. Abram will live there for many years. Sarah will be buried near there (chapter 23), and much later David will be made king there first (2 Samuel 2:4).

Dust is a picture of a number too large to count. Abram still has no child.
passages.later:
Paul widens the promise: “the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world” (Romans 4:13). Jesus says, “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). Meek means gentle and not grasping. Abram, who let Lot choose and received the land from God, is a picture of that meekness, though Jesus does not name him.

Hebrews says Abraham lived in that land “as a stranger in a foreign country” and was waiting for “the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:9-10).

The promise of land ‘forever’ is read in more than one way by Christians. The note on Genesis 12:4-9 sets out the views. These notes take no side, and they make no claim about any modern state, border or conflict.
passages.asks: God told Abram to lift up his eyes from where he was standing. Ask what you are looking at most of the time: what you lost, what someone else got, or what God has promised. Then look again.
